extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, and students/scholars of dramatic theory (readers of Aristotle's Poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing/assessing tragic drama (what incidents, actions, and structures make a good tragedy) based on Aristotle's Poetics and the chapter commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of tragedy: produce pity and terror
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pleasure is that which by Imitation produces Compassion and Terror; 'tis the Terrible and the Pitiful which give it, and not the Monstrous and Surprising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy is not intended to give all sorts of pleasure indiscriminately but specifically the pleasure that arises from experiencing pity and fear through imitation; evaluate a tragedy by whether it successfully evokes these two emotions. (Reference to Plato's Philebus: passions mix agreeable and disagreeable elements.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Means: produce pity and terror by imitation, not decoration or monsters
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet ought to produce that Pleasure in us by the means of those things which he Represents; this concludes equally against those who endeavour to give this Pleasure by the means of Decoration only, and those who mix Monstrous and Supernatural Incidents in their pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on stage decoration, sensational spectacle, or supernatural/monstrous gimmicks as substitutes for genuine tragic effect. Example/anti-pattern: Aeschylus/Euripides' monstrous stage-images (Rage with a hundred heads and serpents) which spoil the piece despite fine speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer incidents among friends/relations (family) to excite pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever happens is either between Friends or Enemies, or indifferent Persons. When misfortunes happen among Friends (e.g., one Brother kills or is killed by his Brother, a Father his Son, a Mother her Son), this is what should be sought after.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select plots where the sufferers and perpetrators have close ties (blood, parentage, alliance) because proximity of blood gives greatest power to excite terror and compassion; contrasted with enemy-vs-enemy which produces only a humane reaction to the accident, not true pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not change received fables' principal affecting facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Those Fables which are received ought not to be changed; e.g., Clytemnestra must be killed by Orestes, Eriphyle by Alcmeon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the fundamental relations/events that give a traditional myth its tragic power; minor circumstances may be adapted, but do not alter the core causal/affective elements that generate pity and terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use received fables but invent plausible conduct (make use of them 'as he ought')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet himself ought to invent it, in making use of received Fables as he ought to do. He should draw from his own wit some means convenient to make it succeed, and find out some probable Conduct proportioned to the nature of the Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While keeping the fundamentals of a known fable, the poet should invent plausible plot-management and probable motives/means to render the action coherent and effective on stage; invention is required but must not contradict essential elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify actions by knowing/ignorant and to_do/not_to_do (four manners)
rubrics_metrics.description: These four Terms — To do, not to do, to know, not to know — produce four manners of Actions: combinations of whether an actor knows the cruelty and whether the action is completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to analyze or design tragic incidents: (1) acts done knowingly and completed; (2) acts done unknowingly then remembered; (3) about to act but recollects before execution; (4) acts wittingly but does not complete. Each combination has different tragic suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred ordering of the four manners (3 > 2 > 1 > 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of these four, the third (person is about to commit a crime but recollects before execution) is best; the second (commits ignorantly and remembers after) is preferable to the first; the first (acts with full knowledge and completes the crime) is more faulty; the fourth (acts voluntarily and knowingly but does not execute) is the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tragic crises so that the strongest effect is achieved by the third manner (near-miss recognition/peripety). Reasons: third engages audience expectation and spares gratuitous cruelty; second still allows passion without culpable barbarity; first can be too abhorrent; fourth lacks passion and is not tragical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cruel actions without passion (voluntary intent but not executed)
rubrics_metrics.description: When any Person goes to commit a Crime, Voluntarily and Wittingly, and yet does not execute it, this manner is the very worst of all; besides being horrible, 'tis not Tragical, since there is nothing affecting in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make the central tragic action an unfulfilled voluntary design (merely intention), because it shows barbarity without the passions that elicit pity/fear; such imperfect actions are faulty and better treated as incidental or epic episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place peripety and remembrance close together for stage effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should always choose the way where the Action and the Remembrance come so near together that the Poet may use them both, without doing violence to his Subject; if remembrance is long after, it is a defect (e.g., Oedipus' delayed recognition is problematic for stage form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting or inventing plots, ensure that recognition (anagnorisis) and reversal (peripeteia) occur within the dramatic timeframe so that the audience experiences both the action and the immediate emotional consequences on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate an entire and perfect action (principal action must be complete)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the imitation of an entire and perfect Action. The principal action must be complete and constitute a proper subject of imitation; imperfect or unfinished actions cannot serve as the principal subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plays with a unified, causally complete main action (beginning, middle, end) rather than fractured or merely episodic incidents; if an action is imperfect, it may be a fine epic episode but is unsuitable as the central tragic plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make danger certain and evident to arouse audience sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be certain ties of Love or Friendship, where the Evils which one of the Persons loved may threaten the other and interest us considerably, but then the danger must be certain and evident; if that fails, the Audience will never be touched with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When staging threatened harms or jeopardy, ensure the audience clearly perceives the risk and stakes — ambiguous or uncertain threats reduce emotional engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize rarity of suitable tragic subjects and reuse mythic families wisely
rubrics_metrics.description: There are few Families which can furnish good Subjects for Tragedy; the first Poets borrowed them from Chance and poets today are forced to recur to the same Families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept the limited pool of high-stakes familial subjects and handle them with care: preserve the elements that produce pity and terror while using invention to make them stage-worthy; avoid gratuitous alteration that undermines their power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect actions may be effective in epic but not as tragedy's principal action
rubrics_metrics.description: Though these imperfect Actions take no place in Tragedy, they have wonderful fine effects in Epic Poems (e.g., Achilles drawing his sword), but they are deficient for tragedy because they are cruel without passion or lack tragic completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your scene relies on an unrealized or incomplete violent intention for its emotional punch, consider placing it as an epic/episodic element rather than the central tragic plot; evaluate whether it evokes passion or merely horror.
